[DAY1 13:19:00 - DAY1 13:19:30]
I turn my head to the right and say, "I've been waiting for over an hour. Finally, someone came." I turn my head left, look down and use my phone, then put it down and ask, "If we set up the second floor, what should we set up?" I sit rocking and sway, shaking my head and gesturing with my right hand. Shure asks, "What?" I continue, "If we set up this second floor, our event venue might be here — this area is quite big, you can move more. Move all the chairs from downstairs up here — sofas." Katrina adds, "It's just to introduce products."

[DAY1 19:32:34 - DAY1 19:32:58]
I scan the second-floor living room, inspect the corner camera and the computer on the floor, count the devices, and monitor the equipment's operation.

[DAY1 19:41:00 - DAY1 19:41:28]
Tasha: "Add sugar three times." I watch Tasha write on the table. "Oh my." Tasha says, "Can't remember," "Uh, no," and "I remember the exact recipe." He looks up the recipe for the soup we're making tonight. Alice: "I'll put this aside for now." Tasha: "Look for the egg pricker," "This, this heart is okay," "Just like this," and "Then note the oven temperature." Alice tidies the table. I turn to look at the blackboard, walk to the entryway, and go up the stairs to the second floor.

[DAY1 19:41:34 - DAY1 19:42:00]
I reach the second-floor living room doorway and walk to the center, watching the devices operate as I pace back and forth. I walk out, go up the stairs, pause to get ready, and slowly walk down. Tasha: "Ta-da-da-da-da-da-da." I go to the first-floor living room door, walk in, and look at Tasha. Tasha: "Can you help me?"

[DAY1 13:18:00 - DAY1 13:21:00]
I used my phone continuously while moving and standing still to communicate and gather information about the venue's conditions. I asked about airflow issues upstairs, and Katrina explained that the upstairs area was hotter and lacked ventilation, making it unsuitable for airflow. We discussed that the weather was good for drying clothes but confirmed there was no way to improve ventilation upstairs. This established the environmental limitations of the venue's upper floor.

I inquired about the arrival of a person with short hair whom Katrina identified as needing to go to the lab for work. We discussed their late departure the previous night and estimated their arrival around noon. We acknowledged the necessity for them to clock in despite the distance, and Katrina noted that it should be manageable if the person drove. This clarified the timing and logistics of key personnel arrival.

While operating my phone, I noted the cameras and mentioned that we had been waiting for over an hour before someone arrived. I proposed setting up the second floor as our event venue because of its larger space that would allow for better movement. I suggested moving all chairs and sofas from downstairs to the second floor. Shure and Katrina contributed to the discussion, confirming that the setup would be for product introductions and including self-introductions in the space. We agreed that the venue might require some adjustments to suit the event needs.

During the venue discussion, Alice and Lucia compared the current location with other spaces, noting size differences and layout changes. Tasha observed my voice shaking, indicating a moment of strain, but I continued to focus on operating my phone and participating in the conversation. This segment captured the ongoing planning and spatial considerations for the event setup.

Shure asked about the location of coffee and who unplugged the fridge the previous day. I responded that no one had touched the fridge, and Shure expressed uncertainty about who unplugged it. I laughed and acknowledged the situation without further resolution. This concluded with a brief check on logistics and equipment status relevant to the event preparations.

[DAY1 11:09:43 - DAY1 12:12:00]
I initiated the group meeting by setting up my phone as a stopwatch and instructed everyone to mark timestamps for recording. After collecting and turning off the phone from Katrina, I led a discussion reviewing our previous day's plans, presenting USB drives and hard drives on the table as backup tools to ensure data security if discussions stalled. This established the meeting’s purpose and prepared the group for the upcoming tasks.

I directed the dismantling of four hard drives placed on the dining table, appointing Shure as mentor due to Lucia’s prior experience with similar tasks. I managed the distribution of power banks and organized data cables, clarifying each member’s role to maintain smooth execution. Upon completing disassembly, I organized the equipment and disposables by placing boxes on shelves and sorting trash, instructing the group on items to keep or discard, thereby maintaining workspace order for subsequent activities.

To support focused discussions, I adjusted the microphone and introduced a screen, strategically arranging the equipment and briefing the group on its intended function. This concluded the preparation phase, establishing a foundation for productive dialogue. I then invited the group to my bedroom, where I displayed my workstation consisting of ten computers connected mainly to six pairs of glasses. I explained the data transfer process that occurs after each three-hour recording session, detailing the hard drives’ dual-cable setup—one connected to the computer and the other to a power source simulating a computer environment—and demonstrated cable management techniques, acknowledging Shure’s observation regarding loose cables.

When Shure raised concerns about potential power outages, I admitted that abrupt power loss could cause problems, and we discussed the absence of backup power supplies such as USB backups. Shure inquired about possible solutions during our reflection outside, which clarified vulnerabilities in workstation setup, data handling, and power stability.

I prepared a small tripod near the desk and coordinated with the group to begin installation, emphasizing careful handling of the fragile glasses per classmate instructions. Following Lucia’s guidance, I examined components, confirmed the presence of screws, and distributed them as needed, facilitating the group’s understanding of delicate assembly and correct screw placement. I moved throughout the workspace to position stands and stools while supporting discussions among Lucia, Alice, and Katrina regarding screw holes and insertion, confirming correct placements.

Addressing concerns about the screwdriver’s magnetic properties, I noted no issues during the day, with Lucia and Shure confirming its non-magnetic nature, which aided the assembly process. I observed the team continuing to fix parts, noting difficulties handling various screw sizes while maintaining focus on proper tool usage.

Noticing that Tasha’s hair was blocking the camera, I requested her to adjust it, and after she complied, I resumed monitoring the assembly process. At Shure’s request, I encouraged playing background music, leading the group to select upbeat songs from Northeast China. I proposed dancing to lighten the mood, which Shure supported while confirming technical details of embedding tasks that I approved. I briefly engaged Shure in a conversation about her hometown to confirm her local knowledge, all while observing ongoing work.

I actively assisted by twisting screws on Tasha’s box, moving between team members and inserting a rod into a black box. I explained the strip’s aesthetic function, with Lucia noting it replaced a discarded part and Shure confirming its proper fit. When Alice asked if the task was complete, the group indicated it was nearly finished.

I unpacked a cardboard box and organized data cables, leading a discussion about wiring experiences among Shure, Lucia, Alice, and Katrina, confirming task roles and lightheartedly noting the need for further training. I carried boxes along the assembly line, placing them across rooms, oversaw screw tightening on Shure’s box, and instructed on item placement, emphasizing proper installation and encouraging self-installation when necessary.

After completing assembly, I declared the task done, prompting Shure to announce that the group could leave. I initiated a discussion on the guest list for our final day; Shure and Katrina suggested using the blackboard, with Shure volunteering to write due to her clear handwriting. I proposed assembling a shelf next and prepared for this task by picking up another cardboard box.

Carrying the box into the room, I searched for a pen and questioned Shure about assembling an item, to which she agreed it was not urgent. Concerned about the missing pen, we repeatedly inquired about its whereabouts. I then moved upstairs with a director’s board, returned, and settled at the dining table as Shure wrote on the blackboard, initiating a debate on “EGO life.” I observed and confirmed discussions about stroke order, guest invitation numbers, and symbolic attendance marks, with Katrina proposing differentiated symbols. Shure then prompted me to lead the invitation process.

During a group session with Shure, Alice, Lucia, Katrina, and Tasha, we collaboratively created drawings on the whiteboard, writing names and code names. I engaged by asking questions and suggesting host code names under characters. We planned to invite four to six guests, marking uncertain attendees with stars. I emphasized target invitee numbers and proposed initial recruitment locally via social media or direct approaches, prompting suggestions like gifting eggs to encourage participation.

Gathered around, we reviewed the number of crew and neighbors expected for the event, with Shure writing down figures and the group agreeing on personnel estimates as the first major planning point. In activity content planning led by Shure, I confirmed completion of questionnaires and responded to prompts, while Katrina introduced eco-friendly crafts using flower petals and acrylic glass, explaining materials and processes. I encouraged creativity, observed the group unpacking materials, and maintained oversight.

After securing the camera setup, I confirmed flower delivery and types with the group, inquiring about additional packages. I encouraged the utilization of talents for flower care, engaged with Shure and Lucia about funding and mindset, and outlined next steps: washing flowers and distributing vases for participants to care for blooms used later in crafts. The group discussed creative applications aligning with a seven-day cycle. I facilitated the transition to the next task involving vegetable leaves, with Katrina volunteering to lead.

Lucia presented an eco-friendly jellyfish lamp DIY idea and proposed a short play related to the project, inviting script suggestions. I confirmed agreement with the plan. Throughout the discussion, I moved between locations, observed the whiteboard, and nodded in approval. Shure coordinated next steps by asking Tasha to prepare props, marking progress in task assignments.

I entered the room, retrieved papers from a box, and handed them to Tasha while moving across the space. During this, Shure questioned the presence of certain props in my suitcase, and I responded briefly. Tasha asked about unpacking an item, which I confirmed remained packed, and she offered a ready-made alternative. This established the task start point: unpacking and reviewing items.

Next, I checked my phone for the delivery status of a petri dish, confirming the purchase but uncertain about its arrival. Katrina reported purchasing peony carnations and the vase’s delivery, which I verified. Coordinating with Tasha and Katrina, I managed and confirmed inventories and placements of materials via phone, ensuring all key items for the activity were accounted for.

At the dining table, we reviewed botanical materials: Katrina explained the fragrance frame and its fogginess; I noted rejection of an item; Tasha introduced her recycled-material seed paper designed for hydroponic sprouting with petri dishes. This completed the review and planning stage for botanical elements.

The group discussed Earth Day designs, focusing on Tasha’s original eco-friendly creations. I inquired about the designs’ authorship, and Katrina and Lucia confirmed the seed paper’s environmental benefits, highlighting the creativity behind the work and setting a collaborative tone.

Alice presented an animal-themed puzzle symbolizing Earth’s harmonious but imperfect living, which I engaged with attentively. The group appreciated the metaphor, and I acknowledged the presentation, reinforcing our environmental educational focus.

Discussion shifted to activity-related prizes and supplies. Shure proposed purchasing hair clips; Alice detailed the prize as a narcissus bulb. I confirmed understanding as the group reviewed current activities, with Alice volunteering for the next turn. Katrina mentioned personal plans related to the group’s coordination, signaling progression in task management.

We then covered a second-hand auction event involving storytelling to earn tokens for bidding on items. I asked clarifying questions while Tasha and Shure explained the auction’s structure, emphasizing environmental protection and the use of small presentations. I took notes and briefly left the room before returning to observe packing as auction mechanics were further clarified.

The auction currency system was detailed by Shure, with Alice and Katrina adding economic structure context. I confirmed understanding that all items circulate as commodities within this currency system.

Event engagement ideas followed, including Katrina’s proposal for social cocktail-making parties on the school lawn and Shure’s offer to prepare coffee. I agreed and noted shared planning efforts.

Regarding scheduling, Katrina queried event duration; I specified an afternoon session starting around 2–3 PM, with drinks and sweets planned but no lunch. Flexibility was emphasized depending on attendance. Weather and outdoor arrangements were considered, with a small yard suggested for barbecue; Shure confirmed plans to buy skewers that day, finalizing logistics.

Food and activity preparations included Shure confirming delivery of skewers, charcoal, and meat for the 21st and assessing cooking skills; I confirmed team readiness. Discussions on ice supply for cocktails resulted in options to request ice from a nearby café or use molds, with water quality suggestions incorporated. I organized these details on my phone.

Scheduling activities was addressed, with Katrina proposing time slots to manage flow; I suggested a 3 PM start and noted auction flexibility. Dancing was selected as a preferred group activity over filming, with logistical notes on participants’ considerations. I facilitated decisions and maintained organization.

The auction planning continued, focusing on coin procurement and storytelling. I agreed to buy real coins and supported a concise event length of about 90 minutes with flexible coin-earning methods. Interactive elements like games, self-introductions, and quizzes were incorporated, with an Easter egg-style coin hunt suggested by me and supported by others. The plan emphasized engagement and efficiency.

Equipment and event material preparations involved my suggestions on music and confirming items like the vase and water bottle. I moved flowers to the kitchen and returned, noting regional manufacturing origins as others commented. We proceeded to discuss written materials and timeline planning, agreeing on adding English versions. I confirmed arrival times and flexible pre-event activities, reassuring that early engagement would not affect data integrity. Shure documented plans on a whiteboard.

In further schedule discussions, I confirmed a 3 o’clock Q&A and introductions followed by a knowledge quiz and self-introductions lasting about 40 minutes, with a quick-answer quiz format. I unpacked data cables from boxes, instructed team members to connect devices, and verified power bank ownership to optimize equipment setup. The group discussed the potential extension of event duration by 90 minutes
